subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Time Dilation Near Massive Objects
description: One-minute skill: Time Dilation Near Massive Objects.

hook.text: Time runs slower near massive objects. A clock on a neutron star ticks slower than one floating in deep space.

buildup.text: Einstein's general relativity predicts this. Gravity warps spacetime, and time is part of the fabric that gets stretched.

discovery.text: GPS satellites must correct for this. Clocks in orbit run faster than those on Earth's surface by 38 microseconds per day.

twist.text: Near a black hole, time nearly stops for outside observers. You'd age normally while the universe fast-forwards around you.

climax.text: Gravitational redshift—light climbing out of a gravity well loses energy and shifts red—is the visible proof of this effect.

punchline.text: Gravity slows time. The deeper the well, the slower the clock ticks.

quiz.question: How does time dilation affect GPS satellites?
options: Clocks in orbit run faster than on Earth's surface and must be corrected daily
GPS clocks stop working near the Earth's poles due to stronger gravity
Satellites experience no time dilation because they orbit above the atmosphere

details.summary: General relativity predicts that time runs slower in stronger gravitational fields — an effect called gravitational time dilation. Clocks on Earth's surface tick slightly slower than those in orbit. Near neutron stars or black holes, the effect becomes dramatic.
details.whyItMatters: Gravitational time dilation is not just theoretical — it's measured daily by GPS satellites. Understanding it is essential for precise navigation, astronomy, and grasping the true nature of spacetime.
takeaways: Time runs slower in stronger gravitational fields
Measured daily via GPS satellite clock corrections
Near black holes, the effect becomes extreme

faq.question: How much does gravity slow time on Earth?
faq.answer: At sea level, clocks run about 1 microsecond per year slower than at high altitude. GPS satellites, orbiting 20,200 km up, gain about 45 microseconds per day due to weaker gravity (partially offset by 7 microseconds lost to special relativistic time dilation from their orbital speed).

faq.question: Could you use gravitational time dilation to travel to the future?
faq.answer: In principle, yes. Spending time near a massive object would let you age significantly less than people far from it. This is not science fiction — it's confirmed physics.
